La peur des wokes : l’inversion de sens: Fear of the “Woke”: How a Word Came to Mean the Opposite
Autrefois un appel à l'éveil face aux in: Once a call to awaken to injustice, the word “woke” has become, in Quebec, a stigmatizing label, a “media bogeyman”
Depuis quelques années, je remarque que: For a few years now, I’ve noticed that the words “woke” and “wokism” are increasingly used by politicians and columnists in Quebec, and always in a pejorative way. I’m thinking in particular of the exchange between François Legault and Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois in the National Assembly, where the premier accused the Québec solidaire leader of being woke. I had known the word and its origins for a long time, but among the people around me, it was often used sarcastically.
Plus récemment, le sentiment anti-woke s: More recently, anti-woke sentiment showed up with force when Donald Trump was elected. Shortly after taking office, he made it his mission to put an end to wokism and wasted no time cancelling numerous programs and grants tied to equity, diversity and inclusion (EDI) policy. In Canada, during the last election, Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre promised to end “radical woke ideology” if elected.
En faisant des recherches sur l’usage de: While researching how these terms are used, I came to understand that they didn’t seem to refer to specific people, but rather to a movement, or even to behaviours deemed problematic. Knowing that the word “woke” was originally not pejorative at all, I decided to dig deeper into why it ended up with such a negative connotation.
<strong>« <em>Le wokisme est un mouvemen: “Wokism is an anti-democratic movement that refuses dialogue and uses intimidation and disinformation to push its agenda, and people are fed up, myself included! ” Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon once declared at a press conference last November. You may have already heard this kind of statement from politicians and editorialists about “wokes” or “wokism.” These terms have taken hold in recent years in Quebec’s political and media vocabulary, stirring up debate and controversy. But what do they really mean? And how did they come to carry such a heavy pejorative charge in the public sphere?
Pour trouver des réponses à ces question: To find answers to these questions, I met with Marilou Craft, an artist, author and dramaturgical advisor who has had her share of anti-woke criticism during her career in the cultural sector. She took part in some very delicate debates, notably the one over the play SLĀV, in 2018. At the time, she had endured multiple attacks following the positions she took.
« J’ai senti que c’était impossible de f: “I felt it was impossible to do my job or talk about art or culture without talking about what affects people who look like me. I was often in a context where I was the only person who wasn’t white. But I felt it wasn’t something I could name. It’s as if I had to put up with being treated differently, but I couldn’t name it, otherwise I was creating a problem.”
Pour nous expliquer comment le discours: To explain how the prevailing discourse on social justice issues has evolved, Marilou goes back to “social justice warriors.” “It’s an expression that was used negatively, but at its root, it’s pretty clear: it refers to people who care about social justice and who talk about it. And it would be a problem, apparently, to keep bringing up discrimination. If you experience or notice oppression and you talk about it, you supposedly become a social justice crusader, and that’s supposed to be a bad thing.”
Marilou fait remarquer qu’à mesure que l: Marilou points out that as the term “social justice warrior” begins to be questioned, other terms like “woke” and “wokism” enter the mainstream discourse. In her view, “wokism” is something very vague that doesn’t really exist, and she says that when the label “woke” is stuck on people, they are saddled with a stigmatizing label they didn’t choose. “These people live through complex situations without being able to talk about them freely, because of the negative weight of that label.”
Le mot « woke » trouve son origine dans: The word “woke” originated in African American communities in the early 20<sup>th</sup> century, where it was used in everyday speech to describe a state of awareness or vigilance in the face of racial and social injustice. It became popular in the 2010s, especially after the death of Michael Brown in Ferguson in 2014, an event that catalyzed the Black Lives Matter movement. “Woke” then became a keyword for expressing awareness of all kinds of discrimination, whether racial, social, or related to gender or sexual orientation. However, as its profile grew, the term was co-opted and its meaning twisted by conservative figures in the United States, who use it pejoratively to criticize what they perceive as an excess of militant progressivism.
Au Québec, l’évolution de la connotation: In Quebec, the shift in the connotation of the word “woke” has been analyzed by sociologist Raphaël Canet. In 2022, as part of a study he conducted with a student, Léo Palardy, he looked at 500 articles published in Quebec media containing the words “woke” or “wokism.” The results of his research show that 70% of these texts come from press groups affiliated with Quebecor, that 45% were written by just five authors, and that a majority of them judge “wokism” unfavourably. More recently, Raphaël Canet’s research has highlighted the role of media coverage in consolidating anti-woke sentiment in Quebec society.
Le sociologue souligne que « l’inversion: The sociologist stresses that “the reversal of meaning is that we’re no longer describing a systemic problem of inequality, injustice or racism, but rather people seen as troublemakers.”
D’après lui, cette transformation, qui s: According to him, this transformation, which accelerated after the Lieutenant-Duval affair, created a media bogeyman, diverting public attention from the real issues. <l1>As a reminder, in September 2020, professor Verushka Lieutenant-Duval was temporarily suspended from her duties at the University of Ottawa after using the N-word while presenting a course outline.</l1> The incident received heavy media coverage and was seized upon in public debates, amplifying polarization around questions of censorship, freedom of expression and identity. It was a turning point in the use of the term “woke” in Quebec.
L’usage péjoratif du terme « woke » a at: The pejorative use of the term “woke” reached the highest political levels in 2021, when Premier François Legault used it in a <l1>debate in the National Assembly</l1> to criticize Québec solidaire MNA Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois. “The leader of Québec solidaire is talking to us about Maurice Duplessis. He had many faults, but he defended his nation. He wasn’t a woke like the leader of Québec solidaire.” A year earlier, during the question period at a press conference, he had refused to use the expression “systemic racism” in the Quebec context, on the grounds that it was a concept that came out of African American struggles. The hip-hop artist Webster denounced that stance. “It’s very easy to accuse people of importing American concepts. They say systemic racism comes from the United States, but the use of the term ‘woke’ also comes from the United States. They pick and choose what they want to import from the United States, or not, to feed the language and feed people’s positions.”
Pour cette figure engagée qui consacre u: For this committed figure who devotes a large part of his work to the memory of the Black presence and of slavery in Quebec, this dispute over terminology reveals a deliberate choice to set aside words that clearly name complex issues in favour of vaguer vocabulary. According to Webster, it’s easier to accuse people of being “woke” than to try to understand the questions they’re raising.
La dramaturge Marilou Craft estime qu’il: Playwright Marilou Craft believes it isn’t obvious who the term “woke” actually applies to. She notes that its use in public discourse falls under what is known as dogwhistling. The term describes a rhetorical technique that consists of using seemingly harmless language that carries a coded message perceptible only to a certain audience.
Elle permet ainsi de susciter des réacti: It makes it possible to provoke specific reactions without openly making controversial statements. “Talking about the wokes and wokism is a way of evoking what people fear, without having to name it, or take responsibility for that social criticism. Wokism necessarily evokes something like terrorism, it evokes something negative. It suggests that the wokes have an agenda or an intention against society, when all they’re doing is talking about what they endure.”
Selon elle, ce procédé contribue à renfo: In her view, this device helps reinforce a hostile perception of those who denounce injustice, while avoiding fully owning the ideological substance of the accusation.
Pour les mouvements sociaux, cette évolu: For social movements, this semantic shift is not without consequences. “The trap is having to defend yourself against being categorized as woke, and therefore having to waste time and energy on a topic far removed from today’s social problems,” concludes sociologist Raphaël Canet.
